taxonomy.note: Current Kew accepts Rhus aromatica with three accepted varieties. Older Texas literature frequently uses Rhus trilobata or R. aromatica var./subsp. flabelliformis; current Kew places those names within R. aromatica var. aromatica. The learner stays species-level while preserving this local name history.

evidence: Hays — UT Plant Resources Center Purola Preserve lists Rhus aromatica among naturally occurring plants.
Travis — UT Plant Resources Center Travis County herbarium index includes Rhus aromatica var. flabelliformis; current Kew synonymizes that name under R. aromatica var. aromatica.
Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center Vascular Plants of Williamson County provides a detailed field treatment of Rhus aromatica.
target_zone_range.guardrail: No county inferred from statewide distribution or nursery/horticultural availability. Synonym-based county evidence is counted only where the synonym maps unambiguously to the current taxon concept.

morphology.look_here_first: Count leaflets first: fragrant sumac has exactly 3. The leaflets are often fan-shaped, lobed or coarsely toothed, and the low suckering deciduous shrub is strongly aromatic when crushed.
diagnostic_traits: leaflets ovate to obovate/fan-shaped, often shallowly to deeply lobed and crenate/coarsely toothed
twigs and foliage strongly aromatic/resinous when crushed
yellowish compact catkin-like flower clusters appear before or with new leaves
often dioecious; female plants produce dark-red hairy drupes
fall color can include orange, red, purple and yellow

confusers.separator: Evergreen sumac has 5–9 entire leathery leaflets and evergreen habit; fragrant sumac has exactly 3 usually lobed/toothed leaflets and is deciduous.

Both can have 3 leaflets, but fragrant sumac is a free-standing low shrub with aromatic often lobed/crenate leaflets and compact sumac flower/fruit clusters; poison ivy is commonly a vine or trailing plant and has a different inflorescence/fruit architecture.
